channel.title: The Beholder's Gazette
channel.description: Your premier source for satirical news from across the realms. All the news that's fit to print (or burn).

item.title: Cursed Ring Bought As-Is Makes Fighter Invest Party's Loot
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: A fighter put on a cursed ring sold as-is before anyone cast Identify, and invested all 3,140 gp of his party's loot by sundown. Sterling is buying in.
item.content:encoded:
A Brindlemoor adventuring party, the Cinderfell Company, bought a cursed ring sold "as-is, no refunds" for 25 gp at Marrow & Finch Curios on Friday the 13th, and its fighter slipped it on before anyone cast Identify. By sundown he had invested all 3,140 gp of the party's loot. I have not been this excited about a fighter since I took up my early-morning sword routine.

The fighter, Bram Hallowell, says he only stepped out for rations. "I came back with a nine percent stake in a goblin-run toll bridge," he told me, while his right hand kept reaching for my quill. He also bought 900 gp of Hootline Couriers shares, put 1,200 gp into a gelatinous cube cleaning franchise, and spent 400 gp on futures in a dragon hoard nobody has looted yet. Nobody bought the rations, so the party ate the prospectus for supper.

Wizard Ilsa Penwhistle would like it known that she had Identify prepared. "I had the pearl. I had the slot. He had it on his finger before I found the page," she said. The ring is a band of dull brass, and the inscription inside, the party now agrees, reads "Compound Daily." Their cleric, Sister Mabry Coyle, scraped together 300 gp for a Remove Curse at the temple. Bram moved it into a mushroom farm's seed round before she reached the door.

Proprietor Odalys Marrow, whom readers may remember from the 5 gp ring of protection sale, is not offering refunds. "The tag said as-is. As it is, it is cursed," she said. Fortune-tellers on the market square call Friday the 13th an omen day, and Marrow sold thirteen cursed items before lunch, a shop record. Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society has declined the party's claim, calling the curse "self-inflicted, by finger."

Some people see a cursed adventuring party. I see the first party in Brindlemoor with a diversified portfolio. Most crews pour every copper into a single asset, usually a ruined keep with a leaky roof. Bram spread his across seven ventures in one afternoon. That is synergy. The party has even rightsized its rogue, Nim Tatterby, who left at supper to "find a party that eats."

When I met Guildmaster Tobrin Ashgrove at a balloon gala, he told me, "Sterling, an idle hand is an unsigned contract." I think about that every day. So this evening I bought 40 shares in the Cinderfell Company itself, at 2 sp each, issued by Bram on the back of a menu. He invested my 8 gp within the minute. Brakka Stonesweat will write that this is a curse. Brakka also thinks owlbears deserve a union.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

• Wear first, identify later.
• Read the tag. Then ignore it.
• If your fighter starts compounding, buy in early.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Salamander Oven Rents for 30 gp a Day; Heat Costs Extra
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: The Grand Feast rented a salamander oven at 30 gp a day, and the heat is sold as a subscription. The Seers' Hall foresees a table of fire. Nyx is thrilled.
item.content:encoded:
Okay. OKAY. The Grand Feast committee has rented a salamander oven from Cinderlatch Works at 30 gp a day, plus a "heat subscription," and I was there for the unboxing! Then, this Friday the 13th, the Seers' Hall looked at the whole arrangement and foresaw "a table of fire." For anyone just tuning in: Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook promised a feast for 2,000 on the Town Green on the 26th, and he has 900 gp to do it with.

The hardware first, because the hardware is gorgeous. It's a black iron box the size of a hay cart, with a live salamander coiled inside on firebrick, glaring out through a little mica window like it knows what you earn. Mana throughput is off the charts. Runic latency between "light" and "lit" is under a second. I held my hand near the vent and lost the hair on my knuckles, which I am choosing to count as a feature.

Then Dobb Wrenfield, Cinderlatch's spokesman, walked us through the subscription. The 30 gp a day rents the box and the salamander. Heat is billed on top. The free tier, Ember, keeps the oven "pleasantly warm," and in this morning's test a turnip came out slightly warmer than it went in and otherwise unchanged. Blaze tier, at 12 gp a day, roasts. Inferno+, at 25 gp a day, will roast a goose for 2,000 guests, should anybody ever find that goose. "Heat is an experience," Wrenfield told me. "Experiences come in tiers." (Yes, this is the same company whose Rope Trick Pod charged me to leave. I still love them. I can't help it.)

I ran the numbers on my slate. The committee signed for 14 days, today through Feast Day: 420 gp before one ember of actual heat. Upgrade to Inferno+ and the salamander oven costs 770 gp, which leaves the feast 130 gp for food, plates, and somewhere for 2,000 people to sit. Plumbrook, up on a borrowed chair, called it "a hot start."

Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor read the contract, asked who had signed it, learned it was Plumbrook, and said, "We are aware of the salamander." Then she went and sat down somewhere quiet.

The Seers' Hall saves its gloomiest readings for any 13th that lands on a Friday, and at dawn it posted the feast's: "a table of fire." Plumbrook read that as a promise of hot food end to end. Seer Hester Vole, who had the vision, was less sure. "I saw a table. It was on fire. I don't know what else people want from me."

My familiar Byte, a pseudodragon who now speaks only in ad copy, sniffed the vent and said, "Heat you can feel. Terms apply." Then he sneezed a spark onto the committee's bunting. Nobody has brought it up. Brother Tumbleberry has already written in to suggest a bonfire on the Green "like our grandparents had," which would be free, and also on the Green, where the tables are.

Rating: four out of five beholder eyes. It's the most beautiful oven I have ever seen, and I resent it with my entire purse.

Damage Report: Knuckle hair: gone. Turnips warmed: 1, slightly. Days left on the rental: 13. Bunting: smoldering, unofficially.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

item.title: 13 Prophecies Contradict Each Other. All 13 Come True.
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: The adventuring party took 13 prophecies into the Undermaw on Omen Day. Six said the opposite of the other seven. By supper, every one had come true.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 3, AND BACK UP IN TIME FOR SUPPER — The Brindlemoor Seers' Hall handed the Fourth Attempt thirteen prophecies at dawn on Friday, before the adventuring party went down to Level 3. Six of them said the opposite of the other seven. By supper, all thirteen had come true, and the Seers' Hall says it has never had a better Omen Day.

Omen Day falls whenever the thirteenth of the month lands on a Friday, and by town custom any party delving that day collects a reading first. Seer-Warden Ysmay Coldharrow says her thirteen seers each gave one, as is traditional, and did not compare notes, as is also traditional. "We don't confer," she told me. "Conferring is how you get vague."

For the record, every prophecy came with a date, and the date was today. After the purple worm prophecy with the typo last month, I nearly wept.

Prophecy 2, "You will find great treasure," came true at the second bell, when the rogue opened a chest holding 340 gold. Prophecy 7, "You will come home with nothing," came true at the fifth bell, when Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9 took its Omen Day surcharge at the gate. That surcharge was 340 gold. Chapter 9 calls it a coincidence.

Prophecy 4 said the fighter would fall, and Prophecy 9 said he would not. He dropped thirty feet into a pit and landed on his feet at 3 hit points, so the Seers' Hall has counted both. Prophecy 5, "Beware the door," and Prophecy 11, "The door is your friend," were about the same door. It was a mimic. It is always a mimic. The cleric fed it a wedge of hard cheese, and it spent the afternoon holding the corridor shut against whatever was breathing on the other side.

Prophecy 12 said one of them would not return. That was the mule. The mule is fine. It took a better offer from a party camped on Level 3, and Ansel Pottage, steward of the Fourth Attempt's hirelings, says it read the contract first, and asked for its feed bag in advance.

Box score at supper: fighter 3 hit points, wizard 9, cleric 11, ranger 14, rogue 8, bard untouched and insufferable. I lost one ten-foot pole, my eleventh of the season, to Prophecy 3, "Something will be taken from you." I rolled poorly on that one and I knew it at the time.

The party's bard, who asked to be named, copied all thirteen prophecies onto his sleeve. He says the thirteenth, "All of the above," is the only one he would have paid for. The Hall charges two silver a prophecy. Coldharrow says the thirteenth seer has given that same reading every Omen Day for nine years and has not been wrong once.

Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society has denied the party's claim on the 340 gold, because the loss was foreseen in writing. The Fourth Attempt has appealed. I asked Coldharrow how the appeal would go. She said she had a feeling about it, and that the feeling was two silver.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Party Hired to Clear Out Kobolds Finds Trapped Picket Line
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: A mine owner paid an adventuring party 200 gold to clear out his kobolds. The kobolds are on strike. Their picket line is trapped. Nobody mentioned that.
item.content:encoded:
The kobolds have a picket line. It's trapped.

Forty-seven kobold miners at the Gullet copper mine, two hours' walk north of Brindlemoor, have been on strike since Moonday. They want one thing: the right to set traps on their breaks. Mine-Master Corwin Haddleby answered by hiring an adventuring party, the Dawnhollow Blades, for 200 gold to "clear out the kobolds." Nobody told the Blades about the strike. They found out at the gate.

Some background for the tall folk. A kobold relaxes by building a trap. "Some people whittle. I rig a deadfall," said Tibbet Snarewhistle, a tunnel-shorer at the Gullet for eleven years. "Fifteen minutes, a bit of string, a bucket. It settles the nerves." Haddleby banned what his notice calls "recreational trapping" after his foreman stepped in a snare behind the privy. The kobolds say that snare was clearly marked. It had a little flag.

Haddleby's contract with the Blades calls the job "an external pest-remediation engagement to restore operational continuity." That means he hired swords to break a strike. I asked him if he knew the kobolds were striking. He said he knew they were "in the tunnels, being difficult." Same thing, said by a man in a nicer cloak.

The Blades arrived Tuesday at dawn. There are four of them. Their fighter, Osk Varrow, made it eleven steps up the mine road before a net dropped on him. Tied to the net was a bell and a sign: RING IF YOU SUPPORT TRAP BREAKS. He rang it. He had no choice, he was in a net.

Their rogue, Lissa Fenwright, spent three hours disarming the road. She counted 19 traps. A pit, two tripwire bells, a swinging sack of gravel, and fifteen more she called "honestly lovely work." Every one held a picket sign. The last pit had a cheese sandwich at the bottom and a note: "Lunch break. You'd know if you had one."

Then the party argued, on the road, in front of the strikers. Their cleric, Brother Amlin Dask, sat down with the kobolds and asked about their pensions. Their wizard, Ferrabel Quint, kept pointing at the 200 gold. "We're adventurers. Clearing out kobolds is practically on the license," she said. Snarewhistle told her the license doesn't say a word about scabbing. Varrow, still in the net, asked if somebody would cut him out. A kobold explained that cutting nets is union work, and the union was on break.

As of last night the Blades had not crossed the line. They hadn't left either. They're camped by the road, eating the kobolds' mushroom stew and debating whether "clear out" could mean "help clear out the paperwork." Haddleby wants his deposit back. The Blades say the deposit went on rope.

The strikers aren't asking for much. Fifteen minutes, a bench, and one patch of ground where a pit bothers nobody. The kobolds who voted to unionize in the Undermaw last month sent a letter of support and a very small bear trap, gift-wrapped. Snarewhistle has not opened it. He says that's the point.

So, to every adventuring party with a "clear out" job on the board: before you draw steel, ask at the gate whether they're monsters or just on break.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Giant Boar Rents Tavern Stable; Innkeeper Names Her Duchess
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: The giant boar bought for Brindlemoor's Grand Feast now rents a stall at the Sleeping Mule. The keeper named her Duchess and took a week's rent. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after midnight on Wednesday, a giant boar walked down Tanner's Row and moved into the stable behind the Sleeping Mule Tavern. Keeper Bess Harrowgate signed her in as a paying tenant and named her Duchess. The first week's rent was allegedly paid up front. Duchess is the centerpiece of the Grand Feast of Brindlemoor, where Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook, a halfling, has promised 2,000 people dinner on the Town Green on the 26th with a 900 gp budget. She is allegedly still alive.

Catching up: the Fourth Attempt brought her back from the Thornwood alive last week, because the contract said "bring back" and never said dead. Since then she has been tied to the bandstand on the Town Green, which now allegedly leans about a foot to the east. Plumbrook said he was "taking offers on a stable." Harrowgate made the only one.

"Four silver a night, two bushels of turnips a day, and she wipes her feet," Harrowgate told me, wiping the bar. "Same terms as anybody." The tenancy ledger has a hoof print in the signature box and Plumbrook's name on the guarantor line. Fourteen nights to the feast comes to 5 gp 6 sp in rent, before turnips. I went through the feast budget again. Still no line for turnips. Now there's no line for rent either.

The Sleeping Mule's actual mule, an old gray named Mortimer, has been moved to the woodshed. "She took the big stall and the mule's blanket," said Wat Huckaby, who was oiling a saddle at the time. "The mule just stood there and let her. I'd have done the same. She's the size of a hay wagon." Harrowgate says Mortimer is sleeping fine. Mortimer allegedly disagrees.

Duchess also allegedly chased every pigeon off the stable roof before breakfast, which makes her the best neighbor Tanner's Row has had in years, and I want that on the record. Also the stable door has a brass latch shaped like a fish. A really good fish. I stood on a bucket to look at it and Duchess looked at me, so I got down. Anyway.

Here's the trouble. Harrowgate keeps her house rules nailed up by the tap, and rule six reads "No eating the guests." I asked whether that covers a feast on the 26th. "She's paid through Tuesday," Harrowgate said. "After that we'll talk." Plumbrook stood on a chair in the stable yard and called it "a centerpiece with a good address, which is a strong start." I asked who was going to tell Duchess about the 26th. He said that was the fun part.

Reeve Fennick's office says it is "aware of the boar." Duchess was last seen asleep on the mule's blanket, snoring hard enough to rattle the tap glasses. The Constabulary has logged two noise complaints since midnight. Both came from the woodshed.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Party Casts Zone of Truth to Prove Innocence, Confesses All
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: An adventuring party's cleric cast Zone of Truth at its own town council hearing. It confessed everything in 11 minutes, and three Burgesses resigned.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party called before Brindlemoor's Burgess Council on Tuesday to answer for damage in town asked its own cleric to cast Zone of Truth over the Chamber, "to prove our innocence." The hearing was set down for four hours. It ended in eleven minutes, with the party confessing to everything and three Burgesses resigning over what they said inside the spell.

The party, which registers itself as the Honest Mistake Company, had been summoned over a burned fish market, a bell tower now leaning eight degrees east, and a goat that the charge sheet lists only as "elsewhere." Its spokesman, a half-elf ranger named Coll Varrow, opened by telling the Council that the company had "nothing to hide and a cleric to prove it." Sister Aldith Crane, the cleric, then stood, raised her holy symbol, and covered the room in Zone of Truth before the clerk could object. The clerk did object. He was told, truthfully, that he was late.

Rules of the Chamber permit any witness to offer proof of good faith. They do not require the Council to stand outside the proof while it is offered. It should. I have written to the Committee on Rules about it. The Committee on Rules, as of Tuesday, is one man short.

Varrow went first. "The fireball was mine," he said. "I aimed it at the fishmonger. I would like to stop talking now." The wizard confessed to the bell tower. The rogue confessed to the goat, and then to a second goat the Council had not known about. Sister Crane, asked by Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor whether the party had acted in self-defense, said, "No, we were bored," and sat down.

The trouble began when the gentleman from the Tanners' Ward rose to call the party a disgrace and found himself adding that he had voted for the owlbear leash ordinance to settle a bet, which he lost. The lady from Upper Mill then admitted she has lived in Gorsewick since spring and attends by cart. The third, the gentleman from the Riverside, confessed he has not read a bill in two years and "mostly votes by the mood of the room." All three resigned before the spell wore off, which the Reeve called "efficient, in its way."

Reeve Fennick fined the Honest Mistake Company 340 gold, a new bell tower, and two goats. "We are aware of the goats," she told me afterward. A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake said the remaining Burgesses have proposed a ban on truth magic in the Chamber, to be debated next week, outside the radius.

For the record: this session's Promises Made stand at four. Promises Kept also stand at four, a Chamber first, and the Council has asked that it never happen again. The motion carried. Everyone meant it.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Carpet of Flying Surge Pricing Hits 40x as the Rain Worsens
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: A soaked party hired a carpet of flying to beat the rain. Surge pricing climbed with every drop, and a 9 sp ride landed at 42 gp. I still love the app.
item.content:encoded:
A carpet of flying hired through Hailrug, Brindlemoor's ride-hire app, charged an adventuring party 42 gold pieces for a three-mile hop on Tuesday night after surge pricing climbed to forty times the quoted fare in mid-air. The Copperkettle Four booked the ride at a quoted 9 silver. Then the rain got heavier, and the price went up right along with it.

Okay. I need everyone to understand that the tech here is GORGEOUS. Hailrug carpets have no pilot. A fare glyph is stitched right into the fringe and reads the weather in real time, with runic latency under a heartbeat. It is the most responsive pricing weave I have ever seen, and on Tuesday it responded to a storm.

"It was drizzling when we got on," said Odda Brask, the party's fighter, who was still wringing out her gambeson when I found her. "The fringe went from 9 silver to 1.5 times. Fine. Over the tannery it started properly raining and the glyph said 3 times. Over the river it said 7. Then it hailed." At hail, the fringe switched to a tier Hailrug calls Act of Gods Pricing, which tops out at 40 times the fare.

The party's wizard, Tamsin Reedle, tried to help by casting Prestidigitation to dry everyone off. The carpet logged the spell as an in-ride weather event and surged again. "I made it worse with a cantrip," Reedle told me. "I've been casting that cantrip since I was nine."

Could they have just landed? The fringe offers a Mid-Sky Disembark option for 5 gp, plus a 6 gp Wet Upholstery Fee that applies whether or not you get off. The rogue suggested jumping. The cleric pointed out they were over the river. They stayed on.

For the record, the job they were rushing to, escorting a wool merchant to Gorsewick, paid 30 gp. The party arrived on time and 12 gp in the hole, so the merchant now technically owes them a loan.

Hailrug spokeswoman Pell Ashgrove defended the system. "Dynamic weave pricing makes sure a carpet is there when you need one most," she said. "You need one most when it's raining. We simply charge for that need." Asked whether a carpet should cost more because the sky is wet, she said the carpet also gets wet and has feelings about it.

My familiar Byte, a pseudodragon who now speaks only in ad copy, has been shouting "Hailrug: Get there, whatever the weather costs!" since I came in, so he has already signed on. I'm close. I rode one home myself in a light mist and paid 2 times the fare, which I am calling a fair price for the mana throughput alone. Brother Tumbleberry will say we should have walked. Brother Tumbleberry has never been late to anything, because he has never been invited.

Rating: three out of five beholder eyes. The fringe is beautiful and I want one as a bedspread.

Damage Report: Gold lost: 42 (theirs), 1.8 (mine). Cantrips that cost money: 1. Eyebrows: damp.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

item.title: Party Pays Winter Inn Bill in Gems; Keeper Rates Them 'Pretty'
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: An adventuring party offered 61 dungeon gems, valued at 6,000 gp, for a 412 gp inn bill. The keeper said 'pretty.' A gem cutter said 210 gp.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party called the Gallant Spoons tried to settle a 412 gp winter bill at the Sleeping Mule Tavern in Brindlemoor on Tuesday with a sack of 61 gems from its last dungeon, a hoard the party had valued at 6,000 gp. Keeper Bess Harrowgate held each stone up to the front window, said "pretty," and sent for a gem cutter. The cutter priced the whole sack at 210 gp.

Let me put that on the Loaf Index, because the Spoons did not. At 2 cp a loaf, the party believed it was carrying 300,000 loaves. It was carrying 10,500. The winter bill alone comes to 20,600 loaves, which covers five adventurers in two rooms since the first frost and, by Harrowgate's ledger, 1,140 mulled ciders. (I asked to see the ledger. She showed me. I have counted the cider column twice and it is correct both times.)

Harrowgate extends credit to adventurers as a matter of house policy, and she took the sack without complaint. "They're very pretty," she told the Gazette. "I didn't say they were worth anything. Pretty is a separate column."

The appraisal came from Ivo Clatterwell, who cuts stones two doors down on Tanner's Row and charged the party 5 gp for the privilege. By his count, 48 of the 61 gems are coloured glass, the sort a dungeon builder scatters in a chest to keep visitors cheerful. Eleven are blue quartz and azurite at 10 gp apiece. Two are bloodstones at 50 gp each. "The big red one is a boiled sweet," Clatterwell added. "Somebody licked it. I'd rather not say who."

The economics underneath are simple, and I wish somebody had explained them to the Spoons in autumn. A gem has no price until somebody wants to buy it. The Spoons valued their hoard by how much it sparkled in torchlight, which is roughly how my colleague Sterling Vanmoor values everything, including a horse he bought last spring that turned out to be two ponies. An innkeeper is not a gem buyer. She wants silver she can hand to the brewer on Thursday. Even a real ruby is a poor way to pay for soup, because whoever takes it has to find a jeweller, wait for an offer and pay the cutter's fee. Bankers call this liquidity. My aunt Marigold calls it "why you keep coin in a boot." (I have stopped laughing at her. I may buy a boot.)

The Spoons now owe the Sleeping Mule 202 gp, and they are working it off. The party's fighter is washing tankards. The wizard is on the door, where he casts light for patrons at a copper a time and has so far earned 9 sp. As for the rogue who picked up the boiled sweet in the first place, he has been asked to stay in the cellar until spring.

What this means for your pantry: before you buy anything with a dungeon gem, have a cutter look at it first, and pay him in coin.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Party Follows Helpful Will-o'-Wisp, Loses 9 Patients
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: The Steady Hand Company followed a will-o'-wisp into the Glimmerfen and lost 9 clinic patients for two days. They came back muddy, and oddly calm.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, an adventuring party hired to escort nine patients to a lantern therapy clinic in the Glimmerfen marsh followed a will-o'-wisp off the path on Saturday evening, and nobody saw the patients again until Monday. The Steady Hand Company says the light "seemed helpful." A goatherd found all nine sitting waist deep in a bog pool, holding hands and humming. They are all fine, and all calmer than when they left.

First, the clinic. Glimmerfen Lantern Rest is a clinic an hour's walk out of Brindlemoor, run by Healer Hesper Vashby. Her treatment is simple: you sit in a dark room and look at a soft, steady lamp until your shoulders come down from around your ears. She charges 4 silver a sitting, which I find reasonable, and she hires a party each week to walk her nervous patients across the marsh, because nervous people do not walk well alone in fog.

This week she hired the Steady Hand Company, four adventurers with good references and, it turns out, no sense of direction. "We'd been told there'd be a light to guide us in," said their leader, a fighter named Garrick Pole. "Then a light came along. It bobbed. It was patient with us. Honestly it was the nicest guide I've ever had." Asked whether the clinic's lamp usually moves on its own, he looked at his boots for some time.

Healer Vashby confirmed that her lamp hangs on a post and has never once bobbed. "I put that in the letter," she said. "I underlined it." She has since reviewed the patients and reports that eight of the nine no longer need treatment. The ninth, Mister Aldous Fell, a cooper with a fear of open water, now owns a pet frog and will not discuss it. The Steady Hands, I am told, will be paid for one escort, minus nine.

Here is the plain science, friends. The old herbals say never follow a light you didn't light yourself. A tally kept by the sages of Candlekeep agrees with them, in more columns: of the travelers who follow a floating marsh light, a little over nine in ten end up somewhere wetter than they meant to. A will-o'-wisp feeds on fright. Our nine patients had come in pretty frightened, so they were a fine meal. But two days of bog walking will wear the fear out of anybody, and a calm patient is a poor supper. The sages think the wisp simply got bored and wandered off. I think it got full.

If you are on that marsh road this month, carry your own lantern and tie a rope between your walkers. If a light offers to help you, ask it its name, its references, and why it is so keen. My friend Nyx says there is now an app that shows a little glowing dot for you to follow. Go outside, Nyx, but please, not into the Glimmerfen. And after a fright like this, I prescribe a slow pot of leek and nettle soup, eaten somewhere dry with the curtains open.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Retired Adventurers at Veterans Parade Kick In 12 Market Stalls
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: Forty retired adventurers marched in Brindlemoor's veterans parade and allegedly cleared 12 market stalls on the way. The pie stand did not survive.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the fourth bell of the morning, the Day of Old Shields veterans parade allegedly left its route on Fish Street when 40 retired adventurers kicked open 12 market stalls, searched every barrel in sight for traps, and looted a pie stand. The constables say no one was hurt, though they allegedly did not count the pies.

It started with the Stiff Hinge Company, a party of five retirees whose combined age the constables put at 362. Their fighter, Ottar Bramblewood, 74, was waving to the crowd when he spotted a stall with its shutter down. "He went very quiet," said Wilma Crook, who was holding a commemorative flag on a stick at the time. "Then he said 'door.' He said it the way you'd say 'wolf.'" Bramblewood allegedly kicked the shutter of a ribbon stall clean off its hinges. The ribbon seller was inside, having a sandwich. She was checked for mimic. She was allegedly not a mimic.

After that, allegedly, old habits took over. The company's rogue, Mabry Fenn, a halfling of 68 with a cane she calls "mostly a cane," went down the row tapping cobbles for pressure plates. Their cleric cast detect magic on a wheel of cheese. The 35 other veterans behind them, marching under the banners of a dozen old parties, fell in without being asked. "When the front rank stacks up on a door, you stack up," one of them told me, before he searched my notebook for a false bottom. It doesn't have one. Allegedly.

By the time the constables arrived, 12 stalls stood open and every barrel on Fish Street had been searched, including the rain barrel, twice. A turnip seller was asked three separate times whether she had "anything else in the back."

Then they reached the pie stand. "They checked the pies for traps," said Harlow Puddingfoot, who runs it. "Then they checked them again, with their mouths." Thirty-one pies were split by a loot system nobody could explain to me, and the company wizard asked whether the crust was "magical or just good." It was just good. Puddingfoot was left holding an IOU signed "the party."

Side note: Bramblewood's parade medal has a brass clasp shaped like a little sun, and I stood next to it for longer than a reporter should. It was very shiny. Anyway.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor, who reviewed the parade from a balcony she was not allowed to leave, said the town "honors its veterans and would also like them to use the route." The Reeve has asked the stall owners to send their bills to the parade committee. Fenn, for her part, wanted to know whether the stall owners counted as quest givers, and whether there was a reward.

Longtime readers will remember the bakery door last week. The constables say this is different, because these adventurers have pensions. Next year's parade will allegedly avoid any street with a door on it. Hollis Delvewright of our dungeon desk asked me which level the party cleared. Hollis, it was a street.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Giant Boar Brought Back Alive for Feast. Nobody Said Dead.
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: The Fourth Attempt took 50 gp to bring a giant boar out of the Thornwood for the Grand Feast. They brought it back. The contract never said dead.
item.content:encoded:
THE TOWN GREEN, BRINDLEMOOR, GROUND LEVEL, WHICH IS NEW FOR ME — The Fourth Attempt delivered the Grand Feast's centerpiece on Tuesday evening: one giant boar from the Thornwood, exactly as ordered. It is alive. The contract paid the adventuring party 50 gp to "bring back" the boar, and nowhere in it does the word dead appear.

For anyone just arriving: the feast has 900 gp and has promised 2,000 guests a meal on the 26th. Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook's 4,300 gp menu lists twelve roast boars at 960 gp. On Friday he decided one very large boar would be cheaper, and he wrote the job notice himself.

Ansel Pottage, steward of the party's hirelings, read me the clause standing next to the boar. "Retrieve one (1) giant boar of the Thornwood, suitable as a centerpiece, and bring it back to the Town Green by Tuesday." He folded the paper. "The ranger read that as an escort job. Nobody asked me. I would have said the same, to be fair. It says bring back."

The trip took two days. The ranger tracked the boar to a hollow under an old oak, which he found on the first try, so I will stop bringing up his map. The wizard got Animal Friendship to stick on her third casting. The fighter held the rope. Box score at the Green: fighter 12 hit points (of 38), ranger 9 (of 29), wizard 22 (of 22), because she walked behind the boar the whole way and recommends it. The boar is at full health and looks pleased with the walk. It also ate my tenth ten-foot pole of the season at the tannery gate. I rolled poorly on holding on to it.

Plumbrook took delivery from a chair. "A live centerpiece is a strong start," he said. "Guests love to meet the meal." The committee then asked who was going to do the rest. He said that was the fun part. The fighter said he had been paid to bring it back and has now done that. The rogue pointed out that 50 gp does not cover the second half of anything. The party's bard, who asked to be named, says the boar "has a presence" and should get a verse of its own.

For now the boar is tied to the bandstand, and the bandstand is starting to lean. It has eaten one bunting pole and most of a hedge. Pottage puts its appetite at two bushels of turnips a day. I went through the budget twice and found no line for turnips. Fifteen days remain before the feast, so the boar needs somewhere to sleep, and Plumbrook says he is "taking offers on a stable." No one has made one.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor came out to look at it at dusk. "We are aware of the boar," she said, and went back inside.

I asked the Feastwarden who is holding the rope tonight. He pointed at me.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Sahuagin Demand Underwater Trade Talks; Envoys Hold Breath
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: A sahuagin trade delegation would only parley on the seabed. Varnholt's envoys went down on water breathing scrolls. The ink did not survive.
item.content:encoded:
A sahuagin trade delegation from the Coldtooth Reef refused to parley anywhere but its own seabed this week, so Varnholt's envoys went down to meet it. Four of them read scrolls of water breathing on the harbor steps, jumped, and sank forty feet to a ring of coral off the Varnholt breakwater. The talks ran six hours. The treaty ink lasted about nine seconds.

The parley is about anchors. The sahuagin say Varnholt ships have dropped 340 of them on Coldtooth roofs over the past ten years. Varnholt, a harbor kingdom that charges a berth fee for anything that floats, says the seabed is technically a berth. Tension opened at roughly sixty siege-days.

Trade Envoy Osric Fallowmede led the surface team. He arrived in full court robes, which filled with air and carried him back up twice. On the third try he came down holding a confiscated anchor. Nobody missed the point. Priestess Ksshara of the Coldtooth Reef noted it in the record anyway.

The handshake: firm, two seconds, eleven claws. No hidden dagger detected. One hidden trident, which the sahuagin call a ceremonial fork.

Then the paperwork failed. Varnholt brought its best iron-gall ink. The first draft left Fallowmede's quill as a small brown cloud and drifted toward the Pellam Isles. The sahuagin offered octopus ink, which works fine until the octopus gets nervous. It got nervous during the clause on fishing rights. Clause four is now a stain on a clerk's sleeve.

Seating took two hours of the six. The sahuagin sit on the seabed. Varnholt's envoys float. Aides tied them to the coral with fishing line, and one junior secretary spent the afternoon bobbing a foot above the table, taking notes upside down. "I was told there would be chairs," she said afterward, wringing out her hat. There were rocks.

Speeches went badly. Underwater, a rousing address comes out as bubbles. Ksshara answered in sahuagin, which carries well under the sea, and her interpreter said most of it was about anchors.

By the fifth hour they had a deal, chiseled onto a slate. Varnholt will stop charging the reef a berth fee. The Coldtooth will stop charging Varnholt an anchor fee of one pearl per anchor. Both sides say they won.

The Varnholt field rations did not survive the dive. I ate mine anyway. Hardtack keeps its shape at forty feet, which is more than the treaty did.

Ottoline Vex covered the parley from a rowboat overhead. Her dispatch reports "a warm atmosphere below." It was fifty degrees down there. She saw bubbles and wrote a mood.

The next round is set for spring. Varnholt has proposed holding it in a large bathtub, halfway. The sahuagin are considering the offer. I am packing more fishing line.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Party Pays 450 gp Reincarnate Upgrade; Fighter Is a Badger
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: An adventuring party paid 450 gp extra so its fallen fighter could pick his form under the Reincarnate spell. He picked half-elf. He is a badger. Bold.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party in Brindlemoor paid 450 gp on top of the standard Reincarnate spell to let its fallen fighter choose his new body, and on Monday the fighter came back a badger anyway. The Thornbury Irregulars bought the Form Selection Premium package at Second Spring Groves, a druid grove franchise with six locations, and they have not stopped talking about the fine print since.

Some people see a botched resurrection. I see the most exciting product launch on Tanner's Row this quarter.

Here are the facts. The fighter, Hobb Greaveson, fell on Level Five of the Undermaw to what his party describes as "a door with opinions." The Irregulars carried him to the Second Spring branch on Mill Lane, paid the 1,000 gp base rite in rare oils and unguents, and then took the upsell. Greaveson's form preference, written on the intake scroll in his cleric's neat hand, read: "Half-elf. A bit taller. Good hair."

He woke up on the altar at 38 pounds, striped, and digging.

"We paid for the premium," said the party's wizard, Pell Rookfeld, holding the receipt in one hand and a gnawed boot in the other. "There was a velvet rope. They gave us tea."

Elder Wynn Fernway, who owns the Mill Lane franchise, pointed me to clause 14(c), which reads in full: "Form Selection Premium guarantees that a form will be selected." The customer's preference, the clause adds, "is recorded with gratitude." Fernway called the outcome "a clean delivery." I call it disruption. That is a vertically integrated rebirth pipeline, and frankly the badger has never looked more motivated.

Shieldwall Mutual, the party's insurer, has declined the claim. Its adjuster filed the badger under "voluntary lifestyle change," which strikes me as exactly the kind of red tape that keeps small adventuring parties from scaling. The Irregulars have since rightsized the adventuring party from five to four and a half, and Greaveson now holds the rear rank, where he has already dug two escape tunnels and eaten a rogue's lunch.

When I met Guildmaster Tobrin Ashgrove at a balloon gala last spring, he told me, "Sterling, the customer chooses the box. The vendor chooses what goes in it." I wrote that on my sword-routine mirror. Second Spring understands this. Its new Platinum Form tier, at 900 gp, lets the customer choose the badger's color.

Greaveson, through Rookfeld, says he wants a refund and his old sword. The sword is now taller than he is. Fernway has offered a 10 percent discount on his next death.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

Read clause 14(c). Then read it again, slower.
A customer who asks for good hair and gets claws has been upgraded. He just hasn't run the numbers.
Never let a fighter die before the loyalty card is stamped.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Discount Sending Stones Broadcast Heist Plan to Whole Village
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: A party bought 40 discount Sending Stones to plan a heist and sold the spares. The whole village heard the plan, and the rogue's apology to the fishmonger.
item.content:encoded:
Okay. OKAY. The Gravelpenny Crew, a four-member adventuring party out of Brindlemoor, bought a discount set of Sending Stones to plan a heist in the village of Gorsewick, and all 40 linked stones in the set heard the plan. One of them was mine. I bought it at the Gorsewick harvest fair for 2 silver, and before anything else I need you to know the mana throughput on this thing is incredible.

So, the deal. A normal pair of Sending Stones costs about as much as a small horse. Chattercourt Stoneworks sells the Chatterbox 40 for 6 gp: forty stones in one circle, so whatever goes into one comes out of all the others. Runic latency is basically zero! The Crew needed four. Their rogue, Tamsin Reedly, sold the other 36 at the fair to "make the money back" and cleared 7 gp 2 sp. Profit, for about one evening!

On Tuesday night the plan went out to every kitchen in Gorsewick and one goat pen. Break into the moneylender Ormand Vetch's strongroom at the ninth bell, take back a silver locket the party's fighter swears was his grandmother's, and leave by the cellar window "nobody watches." Vetch heard it on the stone he bought from Reedly that afternoon. So did the village constable, the miller, both priests, and a goat farmer named Hollin, who keeps his stone in the pen "for company."

Then the stones went quiet. Then Reedly came back on, much softer. "Marta. It's me. I'm sorry about the eels, and about leaving before the dance. I think about the dock a lot." Marta Sallowby, Gorsewick's fishmonger, owns stone number 22. Her reply came out of all forty at once: "You still owe me for the eels, Tamsin." Byte, my pseudodragon familiar, who has spoken only in ad copy since the last Sending Stone incident, sighed and said, "Stay close to the ones you love, now in every room of the house."

At the ninth bell the Crew crept up to Vetch's strongroom and found about half the village already there with stools and a jug of cider. Vetch had moved the locket, changed the lock, and put out cups. Constable Brenna Ostrey asked the party to "please pick another night, the ninth bell is choir," and charged nobody. The fighter got his locket anyway, once Vetch admitted, with forty neighbors staring at him, that it really was the grandmother's.

Chattercourt spokesman Wim Larrowby told me privacy is available. Private Mode costs 1 sp a month, per stone. "The free tier is a community product," he said. That's four gold a month so your stones don't shout, and I hate subscription fees, and I hate this one most. Chattercourt also pushed a firmware glyph Wednesday that plays a little chime before anyone talks. It is a lovely chime. I'm keeping my stone.

Brother Tumbleberry sent a note saying I should try talking to my neighbors in person. Wendell, I did. They already knew about the eels.

Four out of five beholder eyes. Damage Report: Heists foiled: 1. Pies eaten: 1. Apologies heard by an entire village: 1. Eyebrows: fine. Marta: thinking about it.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

item.title: Loot Split: Ettin Porter's Two Heads Each Want a Share
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: An ettin porter hired for one share wants two at the loot split, one per head. His contract says 'per head.' The party wrote it. I'd pay up.
item.content:encoded:
The ettin wants two shares of the loot split.

The Copper Lantern Company, a party of four out of Brindlemoor, hired an ettin porter for one share of whatever they found in the Undermaw. On Tuesday they found 2,400 gold in a crypt. At the split Wednesday night the party counted five shares of 480 gold. The porter counted six. Both of his heads say they signed on.

The contract is the problem. The party's wizard, Osric Vell, wrote it on the back of a tavern menu, and it gives the porter "one full share per head." Vell says that means per hireling. "It's an expression," he said. "Like a head of cattle." Ettins are not cattle. I checked.

"I carried the chest," said Grub, the left head, a porter for eleven years. "He carried the chest," said Mollo, the right head, also a porter for eleven years. "I watched the road for ogres. Somebody had to. The wizard was asleep."

Here's where it gets good. I've seen the party's ledger. They docked the porter 8 gold for two helmets. They docked him two rations a day. And they put him down for two night watches every night, because an ettin always keeps one head awake. That's both shifts on one wage. In my old mine we called that a double, and you paid a double or you hauled your own ore.

So the party billed him per head. Now they want to pay him per body. Pick one.

The party's cleric, Hessa Marlow, called the claim "an unfortunate reading of a friendly agreement" and offered "a meaningful one-time gesture of goodwill." That means a pie. They offered him a pie. Grub took the pie. Mollo refused it on principle. They share a stomach, so nobody can tell who won.

If this sounds familiar, it should. Last week a party promised its torchbearer an equal share of 3,000 gold and paid 20. Adventurers love the word "share" right up until it's time to count.

Tamsin Gorrow runs the hireling board at the Brindlemoor porters' hall and has coiled rope for thirty years. She has started writing "per body" on every new contract. "Then some fool will hire a hydra," she said. "I'll cross that bridge when it eats the bridge."

The Copper Lantern Company goes back down Friday. They need a porter. The ettin is free. His rate is two shares, and both heads say it's firm.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Feast Menu Costs 4,300 gp on a 900 gp Budget; Goose Is 600
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: The Grand Feast's budget is 900 gp. The Feastwarden's menu costs 4,300 gp, and the goose alone is 600. Barnaby has done the sums. He needs to sit.
item.content:encoded:
Brindlemoor's Grand Feast has a budget of 900 gp. On Monday, Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook presented the committee with a menu that costs 4,300 gp, and the goose alone was quoted at 600 gp. For anyone just arriving: Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor appointed Plumbrook last week, and he has promised a feast for 2,000 on the Town Green on the 26th.

The gap between the feast budget and the menu is 3,400 gp. (I have checked this four times. I checked it a fifth time out of hope, and hope did not change the answer.) A loaf at market runs about 4 cp, so on the Loaf Index the budget buys 22,500 loaves and the menu would cost 107,500. Spread across 2,000 guests, that comes to 45 cp a head, or about eleven loaves each. The Feastwarden is planning to spend 215 cp a head, which is nearly fifty-four loaves per guest, and some of the guests are halflings, so honestly it may get eaten.

I have the menu in front of me. It reads, in Plumbrook's hand: one goose, 600 gp. Twelve roast boars, 960 gp. A fountain of ale, 1,200 gp. Cheese, 400 gp. Two thousand honey cakes, 200 gp. Tables and lanterns, 380 gp. Bread, 160 gp. A deposit on the dessert table "longer than the Undermaw is deep," 400 gp. The bread is the cheapest line and the only one I would sign.

About the goose. Wennet Abbeyfield, a poulterer on Tanner's Row, wrote the quote and confirmed it to me over her fence. "He asked for one goose that feeds two thousand people," she said. "There is no such goose. Most of the 600 is for looking." The price covers two nets, a guide into the marshes past Ashenfold, and a hireling to stand at the back "in case it turns out to be a cockatrice." If the goose is never found, the looking is not refundable.

Plumbrook answered from a chair. "Eleven loaves a head is a strong start," he said. The other 3,400 gp, he explained, will come from "goodwill, and the fun part." He also proposed that the temple cast create food and water for the side dishes. Sister Ottilie Brannoch said from the back that she would not be blamed for the side dishes, and sat down.

Reeve Fennick, asked for comment at the door, said, "We are aware of the goose." The menu has been sent to the Seating Subcommittee, by mistake, and it has sent back a note asking for chairs.

My colleague Sterling Vanmoor tells me the gap will close by itself once the feast "builds buzz." The feast is free, Sterling. It builds crumbs. My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, has offered the committee everything in it. The boot holds 14 gp, which covers the goose's nets and nothing else.

What this means for your pantry: eat a large lunch on the 26th, and bring your own bread.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Adventurers Bring Home Shriekers; Tanner's Row Can't Sleep
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: An adventuring party stored a sack of shrieker mushrooms in a Tanner's Row cellar. They spread to 14 cellars, and nobody there has slept in four nights.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, an adventuring party called the Copper Bucket Company carried a sack of nine shrieker mushrooms out of the Undermaw last week, left it in the cellar of the Sleeping Mule on Tanner's Row, and the shriekers have since spread through 14 cellars. Nobody on the street has slept in four nights. I've been handing out blankets and earwax at the Harvest Mother's chapel since Tuesday.

If you've never met one, a shrieker is a fungus about the size of a grown man that screams whenever light or a living thing comes near. That's all it does. Down in the dungeon it's a doorbell for whatever lives there. Tanner's Row now has 140 doorbells and nobody to answer them.

The Company's fighter, a red-eyed young man named Garrow Penhallow, told me they never meant to keep them. "An alchemist in the Lantern Quarter offered two silver a cap," he said. "Nine caps, eighteen silver, that's a round for the table. Nobody said they spread." Keeper Bess Harrowgate agreed to store the sack because the Company had paid its tab in full, "which is rare enough that I didn't ask questions." By the next morning her cellar was screaming at the cheese, and readers who remember that cellar's last tenant will know the cheese has had a hard year.

The spores went through the shared cellar walls the way spores do. Inspector Corwin Tallowby of the Public Cellars Board has counted 140 shriekers and classified them as "unlicensed alarms." He asked me twice what day it was. Even Skorvath, the young red dragon whose hoard lies under the old tannery, has filed a polite complaint. The shrieking carries down to its gold, it says, and it has taken to counting coins at night to pass the time. The Board approved Skorvath's hoard permit on the condition that it keep quiet. Skorvath would like the same condition applied to the fungus.

Now the medicine. The old herbals say a body without sleep turns sour and slow, and they're right. A study by the healers of Silverymoon found that folk kept awake four nights running did their sums about as well as a dwarf three ales in. That matches my chapel: 212 patients so far, mostly headaches and short tempers, plus one tanner who tried to pay me with a shoe.

Shriekers scream at light and footsteps, so keep the cellar doors shut and the lamps upstairs. Sleep on the top floor with wax in your ears. Reeve Maudrey Fennick has posted a bounty for anyone willing to clear the cellars in the dark. "We are aware of the mushrooms," she said, and then yawned for a while. Please don't try to burn them out. Three of those cellars share a wall with a dragon.

My friend Nyx has written in to recommend a sleep-tracking amulet. Nyx, it will only tell you that you didn't sleep. Go outside, Nyx, though perhaps not on Tanner's Row. For everyone else I prescribe a warm milk-and-oat soup with a pinch of nutmeg an hour before bed. And adventurers, please leave the dungeon in the dungeon.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Kenku Witness Reenacts Robbery, Frames Adventuring Party
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: The only witness to a Brindlemoor market robbery was a kenku. It replayed the crime in borrowed voices, including the adventuring party's own lines.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the fourth bell after noon, somebody walked off with a cash box holding 62 gold from Mother Harrowgate's candle stall in Tallow Market, and the only witness was a kenku. The town guard questioned the kenku on the spot. A kenku answers questions by repeating voices it has heard, so it repeated a lot of them, and by suppertime the adventuring party that had stopped to help was allegedly the main suspect.

The party is the Tinderbox Five, five adventurers out of Brindlemoor who had allegedly come to the market to buy torches. Sergeant Bram Oddley of the town guard asked the bird one question: "Who took the box?"

"Who took the box?" the kenku said back, in the sergeant's own voice. The sergeant says this went on for a while.

Then it allegedly did the whole robbery. First came Mother Harrowgate shouting "My box! Stop, thief!" and a coin jingle, then a stranger's low voice saying "Lovely candles. Shame." And then, in the exact squeaky voice of Pim Ashbottle, the party's halfling rogue, it said "Nobody's watching, just grab it."

"That was breakfast," Ashbottle told me. "That was about the last sausage. Ask anyone at the Sleeping Mule Tavern." I did ask. Three people remember the sausage. None of them would swear to it.

The kenku was allegedly not finished. Next it did the party's wizard, Ysolde Fairweather, saying "We meet at the fountain and split it five ways," which she insists was about the lunch bill. Then it did Garrick Vell, the party's fighter, bellowing "I'll hold them off, you run!" Vell says he shouted that at a goose on the Quillmarch Bridge two days ago. The kenku allegedly does a very good goose too.

"I heard the whole thing," said Tobin Greaves, who was eating a skewer of fried river eel at the time. "The bird did the thief, then the bird did the halfling. Same bird. Who am I supposed to believe, the bird or the bird?"

The kenku also did a pigeon. Nobody asked it to. I'd like that on the record. Pigeons have no business in a deposition.

Side note: the kenku wears a necklace of brass buttons and one bent silver spoon, and the spoon catches the lamplight in a way that I would call frankly incredible. I stood there a good minute. Anyway.

Sergeant Oddley has ordered the Tinderbox Five not to leave Brindlemoor while the constables sort out which voices committed a crime and which ones ordered lunch. The Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9, has allegedly frozen the party's delve permit for the Undermaw "pending a voice audit," which Chapter 9 says costs 15 gold per voice.

The constables tried a zone of truth on the kenku that evening. It repeated the incantation back to the cleric, in the cleric's voice, and walked away with a candle.

The 62 gold is still missing. The kenku says it saw everything. It allegedly says so in Mother Harrowgate's voice, about every four minutes.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Halfling Feastwarden Promises Feast for 2,000, Has No Menu
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: Brindlemoor's feast committee has 11 members, 4 subcommittees and no dishes. Its new halfling Feastwarden promises a feast for 2,000 anyway.
item.content:encoded:
Brindlemoor's Grand Feast now has a committee: 11 members, 4 subcommittees and, as of Sunday's first meeting, zero dishes. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor named Odo Plumbrook, a halfling, as Feastwarden, and he promptly promised a feast for 2,000 on the Town Green on the 26th.

The meeting was called for the sixth bell. It began at half past the seventh, after a forty-minute debate over whether a committee could meet before it had been formed. It could not, so the Reeve formed it, and the Burgess Council approved it 9-0, as it now approves everything. The minutes, which I kept because nobody else brought ink, run to six pages. None of them mentions food.

Four subcommittees were struck: Seating, Bunting, Weather, and the Subcommittee on Subcommittees, which met briefly in a corner and recommended a fifth. The motion was tabled. There is no Subcommittee on Food. Asked about this, Reeve Fennick said, "We are aware of the food."

Feastwarden Plumbrook is a halfling of about sixty with the face of a man who has never once run out of pie. He accepted the post standing on a chair. "Two thousand guests," he said. "Long tables under lanterns, and a roast you can see from Ashenfold." Asked how 2,000 people would be fed, he said that was "the fun part," and that the temple cleric could simply cast heroes' feast. Sister Ottilie Brannoch of the temple pointed out, from the back, that a heroes' feast seats about a dozen, so she would need to cast it 167 times. The gentleman from the chair called this "a strong start."

By my count the Feastwarden made fourteen promises in his acceptance speech, including a dessert table "longer than the Undermaw is deep." Since nobody has found the bottom of the Undermaw, that is a large table. For the record, the tally stands at Promises Made: 14. Promises Kept: 1, that the chair would hold him.

The committee did not discuss how any of this will be paid for. I listened for the word "coin" for three hours and heard it once, in a story about a dog. A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the budget "exists, in the sense that someone will have to write one." Procedure would put that on tomorrow's agenda. Procedure has not been consulted.

The Seating Subcommittee meets Tuesday. It has no chairs, the Feastwarden having taken the only one home.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Druid Sells Goodberries for 3 cp; Farmers Demand Bread Tax
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: A druid now sells 86 goodberries a day at 3 cp each, and one berry feeds you for a day. Farmers want them taxed as bread. (I checked. Four times.)
item.content:encoded:
A druid named Sorrel Mosswick has been casting goodberry every morning and selling the spare berries on Brindlemoor's market square for 3 copper pieces each. One goodberry feeds a person for a full day. On Saturday, 312 grain farmers signed a petition asking Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor to tax the berries as bread.

I went down to the stall to do the arithmetic in person. (I brought two pencils. One is a spare.) Mosswick is the druid of the Wet Boots Company, a four-member adventuring party, and as a druid of some seasoning she wakes up with nine spell slots. She spends all nine on goodberry before breakfast. That is 90 berries a day. The party eats four, and she sells the other 86 for 2 gp 58 cp.

Now the Loaf Index. A loaf at market runs about 4 cp, and a grown adult eats roughly two a day, so a day of eating costs 8 cp in bread. A goodberry does the same job for 3 cp. That is 62.5% off dinner, forever, from a woman who carries her inventory in a sock. Every berry sold is two loaves nobody buys, which comes to 172 fewer loaves a day. I have checked this four times and I would like to lie down.

Hob Furrowgate, warden of the Brindlemoor Grangers' Fellowship, does not want to lie down. He wants a levy. "A berry that feeds you for a day is bread," he told me, holding a sheaf of wheat for emphasis. "It is bread in a little round coat." The town's bread levy is 1 cp a loaf. Charged per berry, it would push the price to 4 cp, which is still half the cost of the bread it replaces. I pointed this out. He then asked me to leave his barn, quite politely, with the wheat.

Here is the part that cheers me up. The magic leaves a goodberry after 24 hours, so nobody can stockpile them. You will remember the miller who hid 40,000 flour sacks in a bag of holding and doubled the price of bread. Mosswick cannot do that. She is the only supplier in Brindlemoor who couldn't corner the market if she tried, and the berries put a ceiling on what a baker can charge. When people can swap your goods for something cheaper, your prices stop climbing. The proper term is a substitute good. I have underlined it in my ledger twice.

Mosswick herself is calm about the petition. "It is a fruit," she said. "I grow it out of my own spell slots. Tax my spell slots and see what happens." Her party's fighter added that the berries taste of moss.

Reeve Fennick will hear the petition next tenday. Asked for comment, she said, "We are aware of the berries."

My colleague Sterling Vanmoor says the market will sort itself out. Well, it did: it sorted itself into a queue at a druid's stall, and the bakers are standing at the back of it. My aunt Marigold bought a berry on Thursday and saved it in her boot for a rainy day. By Friday it was an ordinary berry, and the boot is still damp.

What this means for your pantry: buy your berries the day you eat them, and keep buying bread for the baker's sake.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)
